summaries.text: The lecturer is introducing the second lecture of the course and welcomes the students. He reminds them to download the slides and code from the course website.

The lecturer is introducing a new object type called a string, which is different from integers and floats. We will also be looking at how to branch within a program and make the computer repeat certain tasks.

Strings in Python are sequences of characters, which can include letters, digits, special characters, and spaces, and are denoted by quotation marks. The value of a string object can be assigned to a variable using the equal sign, allowing for future reference.

You can concatenate strings using the plus operator, which combines the values of two string variables into one. When using the plus operator, Python joins the two strings together to form a new string.
The plus operator does not add spaces implicitly, so a space must be manually inserted if required. The star operator, a related concept, is mentioned as the next topic to be covered.

Python uses the star operator to repeat a string a specified number of times, achieved by placing the operator between a string and a number. The star operator is used here to multiply a space and the student's name by three, then concatenate the result with 'hello there'.

The lecturer is explaining how to use the print function in Python, specifying that you put what you want to show the user inside the parentheses after print. They are also showing that you can convert numbers to strings using implicit or explicit casting.

You can use commas in the print function to add spaces between values, but this will automatically insert spaces between all objects, whether they're strings or not. Alternatively, you can use the plus operator to concatenate values without adding spaces.

When using the plus operator for concatenation, all values must be string objects, requiring conversion of numbers and other types. The lecturer demonstrates how the print function handles strings, commas, and concatenation with examples of different coding approaches.

The lecturer is now explaining how to get input from the user using the input function, which is part of writing an interactive program. The function takes input from the user and allows it to be used in the code.

The lecturer is explaining that the input function requires a prompt inside the parentheses to inform the user what to type. The user's input is then taken as a string, regardless of whether it is a number or text, and stored in a variable that can be used in the program.

The lecturer is explaining that the input function can convert user input to different data types, such as numbers, by using a type cast in front of the input. This can be done by using int() to convert to an integer or float() to convert to a floating point number.

When the user inputs a number, the input function always converts it to a string by default, unless explicitly cast to a number with int() or float(). Python makes this conversion because by definition, the input command returns a string.
You must explicitly tell Python to handle input as a number, rather than a string. Comparison operators, such as checking if two variables are equal, will return a boolean true or false value.

You can compare variables of the same type, such as floats with floats or integers with integers, but not variables of different types, like a string with a number. Python uses a single equal sign for assignment and a double equal sign to test for equality between two values.

Comparison operators are used to test for equality or inequality, returning a Boolean value of true or false. Logic operators can also be used on Boolean variables, allowing you to invert, use and, or use or.

The logic operator "and" is true only if both variables are true, and "or" is false only if both variables are false. Comparing strings lexicographically means checking if one comes before the other in alphabetical order.

The lecturer is introducing the concept of branching in programming by using a real-world example of navigating a maze, specifically the MIT campus, to illustrate the need for it. A simple algorithm for navigating the maze involves keeping the right hand on a wall at all times, moving in a straight line until reaching the destination.

The lecturer explains the algorithm for navigating the maze, involving four possible actions based on the position of the walls. The algorithm uses simple keywords such as 'if', 'otherwise', and 'go forward' to determine the next step.

Python programmers use intuitive words like 'if' to tell the computer to make decisions, creating decision points in the program. The computer doesn't make decisions itself, but rather follows the programmer's instructions to choose between different possibilities.
The computer checks the condition of an if statement to determine which instructions to execute. The indented code block contains the instructions that will be executed if the condition is true.

The lecturer introduces the "if-else" construct, which allows code to take alternative paths depending on a condition. The code now has two separate blocks of instructions, one to execute if the condition is true and another to execute if it's false.

The lecturer explains that the code can take multiple alternative paths depending on conditions, allowing for more than one choice to be made. The "else if" keyword is introduced to check additional conditions if the initial condition is false.

Multiple "if" statements can be used to check additional conditions, and the first true condition will be executed. The "else" statement is a catch-all that executes a set of instructions if all previous conditions are false.

You will always enter only one code block, and it will be the first one that evaluates to true. Python's use of indentation forces you to write readable code and clearly indicates the flow of control and decision making points.
The lecturer is explaining how multiple conditional statements can be nested within each other. Python will evaluate these nested conditions in order, entering the first block that is true.

The lecturer is planning to apply conditional statements to a game, but it will involve learning something new. A 1980s game, The Legend of Zelda, is being used as an example to illustrate a problem that can be solved using conditionals.

The lecturer is showing an example of a code snippet using conditional statements to change the game background, but it creates a potentially infinite loop of nested if statements. The lecturer is illustrating how this could lead to an unpredictable number of nested ifs.

The lecturer is explaining how a while loop can be used to rewrite the code and avoid infinite nested if statements, allowing the game to run as intended. The while loop will continue to execute its code block as long as the specified condition remains true.

The condition in the while loop gets evaluated as true or false, and the code block's expressions are repeatedly executed as long as the condition remains true. The lecturer is demonstrating this with a simple game where the user is prompted to go left or right in the last forest, and the program continues to prompt until the user types "right".

The condition in the while loop will now continuously prompt the user to enter "right" until they actually type it. If the user types anything else, such as "left", the loop will exit and print "you got out of the last forest".

I've added a counter to keep track of how many times the user types "right", with a twist: if they type it more than twice, they get to build a table and flip it. The lecture is now explaining that while loops are suitable for situations where you don't know how many times a user will input something.
The loop counter is being incremented in a separate line to keep track of the number of iterations. Without this increment, the loop would be infinite because the condition would never change.

The program prints the letter 'p' repeatedly if not stopped, slowing the computer, and hitting control C will terminate it. To avoid infinite loops when using counters or variables in while loops, variables must be initialised before use and incremented correctly.

The lecturer is explaining a for loop, which can be used to replace four lines of code with just two, by printing a sequence of numbers from 0 to 4. The for loop variable n takes on the values 0 to 4, incrementing each time through the loop.

The for loop variable increments to the next value in the sequence each time through the loop, starting with zero. The code block is executed with the variable's value changing on each iteration, after all expressions within the block are done.

You can customise the range function to start from a specific value and/or increment by a certain step, giving you more flexibility than the default behaviour. To do this, you need to provide the stop value, and the start and step values will default to zero and one, respectively, if not specified.

The range function defaults to step being one if only start and stop values are given, allowing the function to increment by one. If a third value is given, it specifies the step and the function will increment by that value.
The loop variable I starts at 7 and increments by 1 each time, so the first value of I is 7. The sum variable inside the loop starts at 0 and accumulates the value of I each time through the loop.
The sum variable inside the loop is now accumulating the values of I from 7 to 9, resulting in a sum of 15. The loop is stopped at 10 as per its current condition.

The loop is incrementing every other value starting from 5, with the next values being 7, 9, and so on, until the end minus one. A loop can be exited early if a certain condition is met inside the loop, allowing the program to stop iterating before the loop's condition becomes false.

The break statement exits a loop as soon as it is encountered, stopping the evaluation of any expressions within the loop. It immediately exits the innermost loop it is in, allowing the evaluation to continue with the next loop or expression outside the broken loop.

Y loops are useful when the number of iterations is unpredictable, such as with user input. A Y loop can be used to count things, but the counter must be initialized before the loop and incremented within it.
A Y loop can be rewritten as a for loop but not vice versa, due to limitations with unpredictable numbers of iterations. This is because you may not know how many times you need to perform a task.
